overview: Andorra is a Pyrenean principality whose institutions developed between powerful neighbors and within communities of mountain valleys. Agreements between the bishop of Urgell and the count of Foix established shared lordship in 1278 and 1288. Farming, herding, ironworking and cross-border exchange supported livelihoods long before the growth of tourism and finance.

periods.title: Shared lordship
periods.summary: The 1278 pariatge settled disputes between the bishop of Urgell and the count of Foix through shared authority. A second agreement in 1288 regulated further obligations. These agreements shaped institutions rather than marking the first settlement of the valleys.

periods.title: Parish representatives and powerful households
periods.summary: The 1419 privilege formalized annual selection of parish representatives. Leading households gained control over the council, while poorer households had limited participation. Parliamentary history here includes changing access to power as well as institutional continuity.

periods.title: Government at Casa de la Vall
periods.summary: Casa de la Vall became the council’s meeting place in 1702. The former family house accommodated parliamentary, administrative and judicial activities, bringing several public functions together in a small country.

periods.title: Reform and political conflict
periods.summary: The Nova Reforma broadened participation among heads of households and separated communal from council offices. Economic problems and struggles over representation continued, including an armed assault on Casa de la Vall in 1880.

periods.title: A wider male electorate
periods.summary: Political pressure brought a wider male franchise in 1933. The co-princes intervened and negotiated voting rights for Andorran men over twenty-five. Women remained excluded from the electorate.

periods.title: Voting rights restricted again
periods.summary: In 1941, the authorities restricted voting to household heads, reversing the broader male franchise achieved in 1933. This wartime restriction shows that political rights could be withdrawn as well as extended.

periods.title: Male suffrage restored
periods.summary: The broader male franchise returned in 1947 after the war in Europe. Women’s voting rights remained a separate, unresolved question.

periods.title: Women enter the electorate
periods.summary: Women gained voting rights in 1970 and eligibility for election in 1973. These changes broadened participation beyond the earlier male electorate and preceded the later constitutional settlement.

periods.title: A parliamentary co-principality
periods.summary: The Constitution approved by referendum on March 14, 1993 places sovereignty in the Andorran people and defines a parliamentary co-principality. Its final provision makes commencement dependent on official publication, distinguishing that step from the referendum.

items.text: The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley preserves shepherds’ stone huts, stables, cheese-making facilities, terraced fields and barns for hay and grain. These structures connect seasonal movement of livestock with food production and storage. Together they show how mountain households coordinated work across different elevations and times of year.

Partly paved tracks and low stone walls link the valley’s agricultural and pastoral places. UNESCO also identifies a communal land-management system with medieval roots and four communities owning land within the property. Maintaining this landscape involves collective decisions as well as individual work; declining agriculture is a stated conservation concern.

Casa Rull in Sispony interprets a prosperous rural household whose family, property and working life formed a social unit. Rooms contain furnishings and tools associated with farming and livestock. Several generations could live together, and better-resourced households also employed servants or day laborers, making the house a workplace as well as a home.

Casa Cristo in Encamp presents a more modest household from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Its tools, stone slab sink and christening robe passed through a family make ordinary work and inherited possessions visible. Preserved domestic objects help explain lives that appear less prominently in political chronicles.

Farga Rossell operated during the mid-nineteenth century, closing in 1876. Its reconstructed interpretation centre explains the conversion of ore into iron ingots and their sale in Catalan markets, including demonstrations of the forge hammer. The surviving industrial site connects local skilled work with a wider trading economy.

The twelfth-century murals of Santa Coloma include religious imagery that once formed part of a church interior. Most were removed in the twentieth century and later recovered for Andorra; originals are displayed at Espai Columba. Digital projections inside the church help show their former setting, but are modern reconstructions.

The government’s historical account connects twentieth-century commercial growth with Andorra’s border position, the Spanish Civil War and the Second World War. Trade in goods and currency preceded expansion of tourism and financial services. This economic transformation changed the setting of older farming and industrial livelihoods.

Casa de la Vall’s entrance bears a shield dated 1580, linking the building with its origins as a Busquets family house. Its reuse as a public meeting place in 1702 illustrates institutional adaptation of an existing building. Later alterations, notably in 1962, also form part of the house visible today.

Inside Casa de la Vall, the former entrance became a criminal courtroom, while a kitchen and later dormitory accommodated practical needs of council members. These spaces show the material work behind public administration: representatives needed places to gather, eat, stay and conduct proceedings. The rooms changed function over time.

The assembly room retains a bell associated with opening parliamentary sessions and the Seven Keys cabinet associated with its archival role. Such objects helped organize meetings and preserve records. The present chamber also incorporates a seating arrangement created during the 1962 renovation, so its appearance combines different periods.

The council’s history explains that the 1419 privilege provided for two or three representatives from each parish, elected annually. It also strengthened the position of leading households. The development of representative institutions therefore needs to be read alongside the exclusion of less wealthy household heads from office.

The 1866 reform widened the electorate among household heads, but retained limitations, including the absence of a secret vote. The council’s account connects demands for reform with economic hardship and concerns over public money. Broader representation emerged through conflict and negotiation rather than a single uninterrupted expansion.

The Constitution states that sovereignty belongs to the people and identifies Catalan as the official language. It preserves two co-princes, the bishop of Urgell and the French president, within a parliamentary system. The document is evidence of a negotiated redistribution and definition of public authority, not the disappearance of Andorra’s institutions.

ending.text: Andorra continues as a sovereign parliamentary co-principality. Its 1993 Constitution transformed the basis and allocation of political authority while retaining the co-princes within a constitutional framework. The imported map’s 1938 to 2020 coverage neither dates the principality’s creation nor indicates that it ended in 2020.
